title: Until we meet again
goal: Accept and decline invitations without giving offense, offer good wishes for almost any occasion, and say goodbye like a Greek.
bekal: decline with a three-step pattern that never offends
tell someone not to with μην

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — A dinner invitation
dialogs.intro: Eleni invites Ana and Nikos to dinner at her home. Notice how Nikos declines: he never says **όχι** once.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Ana, on Saturday we're having a dinner at home. Will you come?
lines.literal: Anna, the — Saturday — we-make — a — table — at-the — house. will — you-come?

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Around nine. And don't bring anything!
lines.literal: around — at-the — nine. and — don't — you-bring — anything!

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I'll bring something sweet — I insist!

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Okay, okay! Niko, how about you?

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: I'd love to, but unfortunately I'm working on Saturday.
lines.literal: will — I-want — much, but — unfortunately — I-work — the — Saturday.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Eleni, thank you for everything. I've learned a lot this year.
lines.literal: Eleni, you (obj) — I-thank — for — all. I-learned — much — this-year.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: We're the ones who should thank you. You've become our friend.
lines.literal: we — you (obj) — we-thank. you-became — friend (f) — our.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I'll definitely be back. Until we meet again!

notes: ⚠️ **Turning down an invitation with a bare όχι sounds cold in Greece.** The pattern has three steps, and Nikos uses all three: **(1) show you'd like to** — *Θα ήθελα πολύ*, **(2) give a reason** — *δυστυχώς δουλεύω*, **(3) leave the door open** — which Eleni answers with *την άλλη φορά*. It's much like a polite refusal in English; you only need to add the Greek words.

**Ευχαρίστως** (*ehf-khah-REE-stohs*) = "with pleasure", the warmest answer to an invitation. Warmer still: *Πολύ ευχαρίστως!* Its cousins: **Βεβαίως** (of course) and **Με μεγάλη χαρά** (with great joy).

**Μην is δεν for commands.** *Μην φέρεις τίποτα!* — don't bring anything! *Μην ανησυχείς* — don't worry. *Μην το κάνεις* — don't do it. ⚠️ Don't mix them up: **δεν** negates statements, **μην** negates commands and να.

⚠️ **"Μην φέρεις τίποτα" is never meant literally.** Turning up empty-handed at a Greek home after being told to bring nothing is still seen as a bit improper. Bring sweets, a bottle of wine, or flowers — and say **επιμένω** ("I insist") with a smile. Just like "oh, you shouldn't have" in English.

**Κάνουμε ένα τραπέζι** literally "we make a table", means hosting a meal. The word **τραπέζι** (table) stands for the whole dinner — a cousin of **τράπεζα** (bank), which originally meant the table where money changers worked.
**Καλά να περάσετε!** = "have a good time!", said to people heading off to enjoy themselves. The reply is *Ευχαριστώ!*, or *Επίσης!* if the speaker is going somewhere too.
**Να 'σαι καλά** (*nah seh kah-LAH*, literally "may you be well") is a warmer thank-you than ευχαριστώ. It's for real kindness, not for the waiter bringing your coffee.

**Καλή αντάμωση** = "may we meet again", a farewell for when you're really going far away. Its cousins: **Στο καλό** (*stoh kah-LOH*, "go well"), said by those staying behind, and **Καλό δρόμο** (safe travels).

grammars.title: Inviting, accepting, declining
body: These three columns cover almost every invitation you'll get in Greece — and in Greece, invitations come more often than you'd think.
after: ⚠️ **Ίσως την άλλη φορά** ("maybe next time") is the gentlest refusal there is, and it still sounds sincere in Greece — as long as you actually come now and then.
**Θα σου πω αύριο** ("I'll let you know tomorrow") is the way out when you're not sure yet. ⚠️ But do let them know; vanishing without a word is seen as far ruder than saying no from the start.

grammars.title: Καλ- wishes for almost every occasion
body: Greeks have a good wish for every beginning, every meal, and every parting. Mastering this list makes you sound far more fluent than your grammar really is.

head: Wish
Say it
When to say it
rows: on the first of each month
to someone setting off on a trip
to someone going out to have fun

after: ⚠️ **Χρόνια πολλά literally means "many years"** and covers birthdays, name days, Christmas, Easter, and New Year all at once. If you can learn only one wish from this whole list, learn this one.
**Καλή αρχή** ("a good start") is said to someone beginning something — a new job, a new school, or a new Greek course. It's also the last line of this book's foreword.

blocks.title: Four things no guidebook tells you
items: ⚠️ **You'll be offered food again and again, and one no doesn't count as an answer.** *Πάρε κι άλλο!* will come three or four times. The sentence that saves you: **Χόρτασα, ήταν υπέροχο** — I'm full, it was wonderful. Praising the cooking matters more than finishing your plate.
**Arriving fifteen to thirty minutes late is good manners**, not carelessness. Arriving on the dot at someone's home just catches the host unprepared.
**Personal questions come quickly** — age, salary, marital status, why no children yet. It's a sign of warmth, not rudeness, and you can answer as lightly as you like or laugh and change the subject.
**Loud arguing at the dinner table isn't a fight.** Greek conversation really is louder and faster, with people talking over each other. If you politely wait your turn, it will never come.

blocks.text: And with that, this module is done. Twenty units ago you couldn't read a single letter; now you can introduce yourself, order food, bargain, ask for directions, tell the time, talk about yesterday, make plans, say what you like, describe being ill, compare two things, and decline an invitation without offending anyone. That's all of level A1 — and more than enough to stop an Athens shopkeeper from switching to English. **Καλή συνέχεια, και καλή αντάμωση.**
